title: "Lecture 16: Core Marketing Metrics"
subtitle: STA1000 - Data Analytics and Metrics

## Previously ...

You can produce almost any number. Block 4 is about which numbers a decision
turns on.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Decompose revenue into the factors marketing can move
- Calculate acquisition cost, lifetime value, ROAS and contribution
- Explain the relationship between them, and which one a CFO recognises
- Identify when a metric is being gamed, including by you

# 1. Which Number Is the Business

## Two Laws

**First law**: no customers, no business.

No customers → no revenue → no profit → no business.

. . .

**Second law**: more customers, more profit.

. . .

The second is an empirical tendency rather than a logical necessity. Individual
customers can be unprofitable, and we will spend part of this lecture on the
ones who are.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Which functions in a business can afford to ignore customers? Whose budget is
justified by a number that is not a customer count?
:::

## Revenue, Decomposed

Any brand's revenue can be written as a chain of ratios:

$$\text{Revenue} = \underbrace{\text{stores}}_{\text{distribution}} \times
\underbrace{\frac{\text{customers}}{\text{store}}}_{\text{reach}} \times
\underbrace{\frac{\text{transactions}}{\text{customer}}}_{\text{frequency}} \times
\underbrace{\frac{\text{spend}}{\text{transaction}}}_{\text{basket}}$$

. . .

Four levers. Marketing teams argue endlessly about which one to pull.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Before the next slide: which of the four do you expect to explain most of the
variation in revenue across firms?
:::

## The Answer Is Customer Count

Work on the full US Visa transaction panel, over a trillion dollars of spending
across 32 billion transactions, regressed each factor against merchant revenue.

. . .

**Unique customers per store explains 68 to 84% of the variation in merchant
revenue.** Far more than transaction frequency or basket size, and the result
holds across sectors.

. . .

This is why serious firms measure at the **customer level** rather than the
store, visit or transaction level. It is also why the metrics in the rest of
this lecture are all customer metrics.

<!-- Speaker notes: the students' instinct is usually basket size, because that
     is the lever a marketer feels in control of. The result reframes the whole
     block: acquisition and retention dominate, and everything else is trim. -->

## Vocabulary, Fixed Now

| Level | Unit | Typical metric |
|---|---|---|
| Market | The category | Size, growth, share |
| Customer | A person | CAC, LTV, retention, RFM |
| Product | A SKU or service | Margin, attach rate |
| Transaction | An order | AOV, units per order |

. . .

**Most bad marketing arguments are two people using metrics from different
levels.** "Our AOV is up" and "our customer count is down" can both be true, and
only one of them decides whether the business survives.

# 2. Cost

## Customer Acquisition Cost

$$\text{CAC} = \frac{\text{acquisition spend}}{\text{new customers acquired}}$$

. . .

**The numerator is an argument.** Media only? Media plus agency fees? Plus the
salaries of the people who made the ads? Plus the discount you gave to close the
first sale?

. . .

Every one of those is defensible and they produce numbers that differ by a
factor of three. **State the definition beside the number, every time.**

## Blended and Paid CAC {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Blended CAC**

All spend ÷ all new customers, organic ones included.

Flatters you. Useful for asking "what does growth cost us overall".
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Paid CAC**

Paid spend ÷ customers attributed to paid.

Honest about the marginal channel. Depends entirely on attribution, which is
Lecture 18's problem.
:::
::::

. . .

Reporting blended CAC while making a decision about paid spend is one of the
most common and most expensive confusions in the discipline.

## Cost per What

CPM, CPC, CPA, CPL: the same spend divided by a different denominator.

. . .

Each choice of denominator is a **strategic claim** about what you are buying:

- **CPM** claims you are buying attention
- **CPC** claims you are buying visits
- **CPA** claims you are buying customers
- **CPL** claims you are buying the chance of a conversation

. . .

A channel can be cheap on one and ruinous on the next. The ranking of your
channels changes with the denominator, which is why everyone quotes the
denominator that flatters their channel.

# 3. Value

## Lifetime Value

Start simple:

$$\text{LTV} = \text{AOV} \times \text{frequency} \times \text{lifespan} \times \text{margin}$$

. . .

Then say it properly, with retention and the cost of capital:

$$\text{CLV} = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{m_t \, r^t}{(1+i)^t}$$

$m_t$ = contribution margin in period $t$, $r$ = retention probability, $i$ =
cost of capital, $T$ = horizon.

. . .

$m$ and $r$ are **observable in past data**. The values you put in the formula
are **predictions**. That distinction is the whole subject.

## A Worked Example {.smaller}

A tennis club:

- Annual membership fee: €300
- Average additional spend per member per year: €100
- Contribution margin on that additional spend: 60%
- Annual retention: 80%. Cost of capital: 15%

. . .

$m = 300 + 0.6 \times 100 = 360$

. . .

| Horizon | CLV |
|---|---|
| $T=1$ | €360 |
| $T=2$ | $360 + \frac{360 \times 0.8}{1.15} =$ €610 |
| $T=3$ | $360\left(1 + \frac{0.8}{1.15} + \frac{0.64}{1.3225}\right) =$ €785 |

. . .

Notice how quickly it asymptotes. **Extending the horizon adds less than people
expect**, and adds prediction error faster than it adds value.

## The Horizon Is a Judgement Call

$T$ is conventionally set to three years, for no better reason than convention.

. . .

Amazon has long argued that a seven-year horizon lets it justify investments
competitors cannot match. That is a real strategic advantage and it comes
entirely from a choice of $T$.

. . .

**The horizon, the retention rate and the discount rate are all assumptions.**
Change any one and the answer moves. Report the three, and report the answer at
two horizons.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
A longer horizon makes more marketing spend look justified. Who in an
organisation benefits from choosing a longer $T$, and who checks?
:::

## Using CLV to Decide

A campaign is worth running if $\text{CAC} < \text{CLV}$, with two caveats
attached.

. . .

**The tennis club and the billboard.** €20,000 for a billboard seen by 100,000
people, expected conversion 0.1%.

. . .

Customers acquired: $100{,}000 \times 0.001 = 100$.

CAC = $20{,}000 / 100 =$ **€200**.

. . .

Below the one-year CLV of €360. On paper, a clear yes.

## The Two Caveats

**One.** The rule holds only if the newly acquired customers have CLV at least
equal to the existing average. Cheaply acquired customers usually do not: the
people a discount brings in are the people a discount brings in.

. . .

**Two.** Nobody believes the 0.1%. So firms impose a **fudge factor**, requiring
$\text{CLV} > f \times \text{CAC}$ with $f$ typically 3 or 7.

. . .

The 3:1 rule of thumb you will read on marketing blogs **is that fudge factor**,
detached from its reasoning and presented as a law. It is a speed bump against
optimistic conversion forecasts, not a target to hit.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
How confident are you in a 0.1% conversion prediction for a billboard? Can you
get your money back if it underperforms? Are there better uses of €20,000? Those
three questions are what the fudge factor is standing in for.
:::

## Payback Period

Often more useful than the ratio, because it is about **cash** rather than
theory.

. . .

"We recover CAC in four months" is a statement a finance director can act on.
"Our LTV:CAC is 3.2" requires them to accept your retention assumption, your
horizon and your discount rate first.

. . .

At a payback of 18 months, a growing company runs out of money while being
profitable on paper. This is the most common way a well-measured business dies.

## CLV Cautions

- **Identity is mismeasured.** Can you link the same person across two cards,
  two devices, two email addresses? Every failure to link splits one loyal
  customer into two churned ones and destroys your retention estimate
- **CLV is predictive, not prescriptive.** It contains no model of *why* anyone
  buys. It cannot tell you what to change
- **It can be self-fulfilling.** Treat a customer as low value, give them a worse
  experience, and watch them behave like a low-value customer

. . .

The guiding principle: **using CLV to create more value for the customer
benefits everyone. Using it purely to extract margin sets your interests against
theirs**, and customers eventually notice.

## Firing Customers

In the 2000s consultancies published claims that 20 to 30% of customers were
unprofitable, and firing them sounded free.

. . .

Firms tried it: paying cardholders to close accounts, quietly withdrawing
promotions, minimum balances and fees designed to drive accounts away,
suspending frequent returners.

. . .

Concentration can be extreme. In published work on online gambling, roughly 3%
of customers generated half of net revenue, and the top 5% of winners cost
operators around a fifth of it.

. . .

**Customers talk to each other.** The better move is usually to redesign the
offer and the pricing so unprofitable customers either become profitable or
select themselves out, rather than being shown the door.

# 4. Return

## ROAS

$$\text{ROAS} = \frac{\text{revenue attributed to ads}}{\text{ad spend}}$$

Simple, universal, comparable across campaigns, and misleading in three separate
ways at once.

## Why ROAS Is Not Profit

<!-- Speaker notes: a 4x ROAS on a product with a 20% margin is a loss. This
     single point is the most commercially useful thing in the lecture. Make
     them compute it rather than showing them. -->

A campaign returns **4x ROAS**. €10,000 spend, €40,000 revenue. Everyone is
delighted.

. . .

The product carries a **20% contribution margin**.

. . .

Gross contribution: $40{,}000 \times 0.20 = €8{,}000$.

Media cost: €10,000.

. . .

**Result: a loss of €2,000.** The break-even ROAS on a 20% margin is 5x, and
nobody in the room knew it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Break-even ROAS is $1/\text{margin}$. What is yours? If you do not know your
contribution margin, what exactly does your ROAS target mean?
:::

## Contribution Margin

$$\text{Contribution} = \text{revenue} - \text{variable costs} - \text{media}$$

. . .

Revenue minus the costs that scale with the sale: goods, payment fees, delivery,
returns, support. Then media.

. . .

**This is the number a CFO recognises**, and translating your ROAS into it is the
single most useful thing you can do to be taken seriously outside the marketing
function.

## Incrementality

A brand-search campaign reports 12x ROAS. It bids on your own company name.

. . .

Most of those people were going to arrive anyway. The campaign is charging you
for traffic you already had.

. . .

**Incrementality asks the only question that matters**: what would have happened
if we had not run this? ROAS cannot answer it, attribution models cannot answer
it, and Lectures 18 and 19 are about the two ways to try.

# 5. Gaming

## Every Metric Becomes a Target {.smaller}

Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

In marketing, specifically:

- **Bidding on your own brand terms**, which buys traffic you had, at excellent
  reported ROAS
- **Retargeting cart abandoners** and claiming the sale they were going to
  complete
- **Counting assisted conversions** in every channel that touched them, so the
  channel totals exceed the actual conversions
- **Moving the attribution window** until the number improves
- **Redefining "new customer"** near the end of the quarter

. . .

None of these requires dishonesty. Each is a defensible choice made repeatedly
in the same direction.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Which of these could you do to your own portfolio, honestly, and improve every
number in your final report? Is there a check that would catch it?
:::

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

For a business of your choice, or your portfolio:

1. Calculate CAC and CLV with every assumption written down
2. Compute CLV at $T=1$ and $T=3$ and say how much the horizon is worth
3. Compute ROAS, then break-even ROAS, then contribution for the same campaign
4. Identify the assumption your conclusion is most sensitive to
5. Describe how someone could make this campaign look excellent while losing
   money

**25 minutes**

# 6. AI as Devil's Advocate

## AI This Block: An analyst you interrogate

Where we are on the module's AI spine, introduced in Lecture 10:

> **An analyst you interrogate**

## The Block 4 Step on the Spine

From here on, the useful prompt is not "do this" but **"tell me why I am
wrong"**.

> "I am reporting a 4.2x ROAS on this campaign and recommending we increase
> spend. Argue against that recommendation. Assume I have not thought about
> margin, incrementality or the quality of the customers this channel acquires."

. . .

Naming the objections you have already considered forces it past the obvious
three and into the ones you have not.

## Why This Works

The standard objections to a marketing metric are **well documented**, which
means a broadly-read assistant reproduces them reliably and quickly.

. . .

What it cannot know is which objection applies to **your** numbers: your margin,
your channel mix, your customers, your data.

. . .

**You supply the context, it supplies the checklist.** That division of labour is
the whole of block 4.

## Where It Will Be Confidently Wrong

- It will accept your CAC definition without asking what is in the numerator
- It will quote the 3:1 LTV:CAC rule as though it were a finding rather than a
  fudge factor
- It will not notice that your retention rate came from 12 users
- It will produce a beautifully argued case against a number you typed in wrong

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
It will argue whichever side you ask it to, with equal fluency. What does that
tell you about how much weight its agreement should carry?
:::

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

1. Compute CAC, CLV and ROAS for a campaign
2. Ask an assistant to argue that your conclusion is wrong
3. Identify which of its objections actually applies to your numbers, and which
   are generic
4. Recompute with the applicable objection addressed
5. Then ask it to argue the **opposite** case and notice how good that one also
   sounds

**15 minutes**
